extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers / creative-writing students / workshop participants
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and evaluative criteria for writing and revising narrative prose (sentence, punctuation, paragraph, rhythm, and repetition), aimed at workshop practice and exercises. Focus is on clarity, intentional use of rules, and the craft-level choices that shape readable fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral duty to use language thoughtfully
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer’s moral duty is to use language thoughtfully and well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misuse of language (lying or careless ignorance) breeds half-truths, misunderstandings, and lies. Because the reader has only the words, writers must take responsibility for clarity; sloppy grammar/punctuation can cripple meaning and even invalidate a story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the rules before you break them
rubrics_metrics.description: If writing breaks rules, it must do so intentionally and consistently: 'To break a rule you have to know the rule. A blunder is not a revolution.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate dialectal or voice-based 'incorrect' usage is acceptable when skillful and consistent; accidental incorrect usage is disastrous. Example: dialectical punctuation may be 'incorrect' but punctuation must still be impeccable to keep cadence clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity for the reader (reader has only the words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing standards differ from speaking because, in print, the reader lacks voice and intonation and therefore the words must be clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electronic/instant writing often assumes spoken understanding and so causes misreading and quarrels; emoticons are poor substitutes for communicating feelings. Always revise to ensure the words alone convey intended meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation’s purpose: shape rhythm and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Wise punctuation keeps the flow running clear; careless punctuation makes a written sentence unclear and ugly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study punctuation in admired prose to see why an author pauses or breaks a sentence; experiment (e.g., write without punctuation then punctuate later) to learn how punctuation establishes rhythm and meaning. Example exercise: write a paragraph with no punctuation and later punctuate it to see which version works better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence’s chief duty: lead to the next sentence (coherence)
rubrics_metrics.description: In narrative, the chief duty of a sentence is to lead to the next sentence; above all a sentence needs coherence and must 'hang together.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incoherent or patched-together sentences cannot lead seamlessly; they may need slight rearrangement or full rewrite. Evaluate sentences by whether they hold themselves together and carry the reader forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misplacement (misplaced modifiers) as a common sentence problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Parts of a sentence must fit together in the best possible order; misplaced elements distort meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect by rereading and revise by reordering or rewriting. Examples: 'She fell down as she stood up and broke her nose.' or 'He was sure when the test came he could pass it.' Consider how to rephrase to remove ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danglers (dangling modifiers) are harmful
rubrics_metrics.description: Dangling modifiers (e.g., 'Leaving the house, a giant oak towered over them.') can wreck the scenery or create nonsense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most writers leave some danglers; catch them in revision by ensuring the grammatical subject matches the modifier or by restructuring the sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'conjunctivitis' (overuse of conjunctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stringing short sentences together with conjunctions naively creates an infantile droning that makes the story hard to follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conjunction chains can be a deliberate style but used naively they bore and confuse. Vary sentence structure rather than defaulting to many 'and/and/and' links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sentences that stop the story (ornamental distractions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence that is so unexpected, ornate, or striking that it stops the reader to admire it is failing as a narrative sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance ornament and function: striking adjectives/adverbs/similes that interrupt forward motion should be cut or moved ('kill your darlings'). Poetry can pause for beauty; prose's beauty lives in the whole work's movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence rhythm and variety (no single optimum length)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no optimum sentence length; the optimum is variety—sentence length is established by contrast and interplay with surrounding sentences and by what the sentence says and does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use short sentences for impact and long sentences for complex thought, but mix deliberately. In revision, check for rhythm and play with sentence lengths to avoid monotony (all short = choppy; all long = clogging).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage long, complex sentences carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Long complex sentences must be solidly constructed and their connections must be clear so the reader doesn't get lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long syntax acts like muscles and sinews of narrative—use semicolons, careful clause management, and readable anchoring. Evaluate long sentences for assured syntax and flow; if the reader must go back, the sentence needs work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short-sentence constraint: naturalness and grammatical completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Short sentences must still read naturally and (when required by an exercise) be complete (subject + verb).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise guidance: write 100–150 words in sentences of seven or fewer words, no sentence fragments—then critique whether the short sentences fit the story and read naturally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-sentence constraint: clarity of construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Very long single sentences must be constructed in clear, articulated pieces or in a controlled torrent so the reader can follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise guidance: write up to 350 words as one sentence; in critique, ask whether it is built from clear sub-pieces or one torrent, and whether syntax is clear and the reader doesn't get lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraphing: use contextual judgment, not arbitrary rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules like 'no paragraph should have more than four sentences' are rubbish; paragraphing depends on medium and the structure of the prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paragraph indents show connections and separations; let paragraphing serve the structure and rhythm of the work. If publishing in magazines, editors may change breaks to fit columns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition: use as an intentional rhythmic and structural device
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition (words, phrases, images, events) is not inherently bad; it's the central means of achieving rhythm and structural echo in narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate accidental/awkward repetition (fixable in revision) from deliberate repetition used for incantation, emphasis, or structural patterning (e.g., folktales, Dickens, Micawber). Use thesaurus sparingly and discreetly; don't avoid repetition simply to avoid repeating words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural repetition and foreshadowing
rubrics_metrics.description: Structural repetition is the similarity of events or images echoed across a story and is a major device for foreshadowing and development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for and plan recurring images/events; they can shape the whole novel (example: first chapter of Jane Eyre introducing material that returns). In critique, assess effectiveness and subtlety/obviousness of repetitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for critiquing experimental exercises (unpunctuated / repetition)
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating workshop exercises (e.g., unpunctuated paragraph, repetition exercises), ask specific questions about comprehensibility, fit of technique to subject, and what the exercise revealed about the writer's process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample critique questions: For unpunctuated piece—How comprehensible was it without the author’s voice? To what extent did the unpunctuated flow shape the narrative? Was the process valuable? Was the result readable? For repetition exercises—concentrate on effectiveness and subtlety of repetitions and whether they brought out feeling-tone or structure.
